name: Supply-side progressivism
summary: Supply-side progressivism is the liberal-left view, named by Ezra Klein in 2021 and developed in Klein and Thompson's Abundance (2025), that affordability and progress depend on building more of what people need (housing, clean energy, public infrastructure, scientific discovery) rather than only subsidising demand. It blames rules, vetoes and capture by incumbents for manufactured scarcity, wants government made capable of finishing projects, and keeps redistribution alongside supply reform.
scope: The abundance agenda as its American proponents state it: Klein's term 'supply-side progressivism' (also called supply-side liberalism, the abundance agenda or Abundance faction), as set out by Klein and Thompson in their Lex Fridman interview on the book and described by Saldin and Teles and by Levitz. It excludes Reagan-era supply-side economics, Tyler Cowen's state-capacity libertarianism (which Saldin and Teles say does not align on all issues), and the authors' personal views on Trump, DOGE, foreign affairs or AI. Statements outside housing, energy, science, state capacity and the redistribution that Klein and Thompson pair with them are left unanswered.

local-veto-new-housing.rationale: Thompson tells mayors to stand against a hearing room of objectors and approve housing, and Saldin and Teles endorse moving zoning power away from local opponents of building; consultation stays, the veto does not.

limit-growth.rationale: Thompson says the climate challenge is not getting people to use less electricity but building a great deal of clean energy so people can keep modern lives, and Saldin and Teles contrast this with the technology scepticism of degrowth.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Saldin and Teles say wind and solar must be joined by massive geothermal and nuclear capacity, and Klein calls a national goal for new nuclear capacity a very important proposal.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Thompson names expanding the earned income tax credit, with the child tax credit, as essential demand-side policy that goes alongside supply reform.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Klein says he is for more redistribution than now and Thompson calls redistributing income from the rich to the poor essential, though neither names a rate for taxes on the wealthy.

cut-welfare.rationale: Thompson says expanding cash welfare might be essential to cutting poverty, and Saldin and Teles want a simpler, more effective welfare state, which runs against cutting welfare.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: The sources call for huge, rapid public action to build clean power and transmission, while not saying the whole climate response must be drastic government action.

human-caused-global-warming.rationale: Thompson treats global warming as the reason to build clean energy at scale, and a call to decarbonize presupposes that emissions drive warming.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Klein says he does not want a coal-fired power plant to be buildable in America, and the agenda is built around decarbonizing by building clean supply instead.

accelerate-technology.rationale: The agenda wants to pull innovation forward by clearing the rules that slow deployment and rethinking how government acts, but the sources do not discuss disruption to institutions as a price worth paying.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Klein says that in many cases government should deregulate markets and in many it should regulate more, and the agenda is mainly about the rules government applies to itself.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Klein says price signals work in places and bring on more supply, but that markets cannot tell coal wealth from solar wealth and that redistribution and public funding are part of the agenda.

unions-good.rationale: Klein backs a stronger labor movement and sectoral bargaining and calls unions a natural ally, while Saldin and Teles name public-employee unions among the producer interests the agenda will fight, and Levitz notes supply-side liberals may differ on labor standards.

missingStatements.text: Subsidising demand for a good while its supply stays restricted drives its price up.
missingStatements.rationale: Klein and Thompson both argue that rental vouchers and tuition grants without more housing or more places only raise prices, as the interview's central example of cost-disease socialism.

quotes.text: We do rental vouchers, giving people rental vouchers in the San Francisco housing market, unless you build more housing, just creates something that our friends at the Niskanen Center call cost disease socialism, where you are increasing demand for good at which you’ve constricted supply. If you do that, you’re just going to drive the price up.
quotes.where: Lex Fridman interview, Klein, 01:18:32, line 403 of the saved text

quotes.text: And if your only policy on housing is to increase housing vouchers without increasing the supply of housing, macroeconomically speaking, there’s only one direction for housing prices to go, and it’s straight up to the moon.
quotes.where: Lex Fridman interview, Thompson, 01:19:26, line 408 of the saved text

missingStatements.text: Zoning rules should be loosened to allow more housing.
missingStatements.rationale: Thompson blames zoning and historic-preservation rules for scarce housing and welcomes California's changes to its laws, and Saldin and Teles treat zoning governance as the heart of the housing crisis and back the YIMBY push to strip it of its power to block building.

quotes.text: we have rules, zoning rules, historic preservation rules, permitting processes, environmental reviews, laws that we created that have gotten in the way of making abundant the most important material good there is, which is housing.
quotes.where: Lex Fridman interview, Thompson, 01:09:55, line 372 of the saved text

quotes.text: At the heart of this problem is our system of housing governance, which combines all of the worst features of localism and vetocracy.
quotes.where: Saldin and Teles, section on the abundance agenda, line 66 of the saved text

missingStatements.text: Environmental review and permitting rules should be reformed to speed up construction.
missingStatements.rationale: Saldin and Teles call the permitting and review regime in need of thoroughgoing reform, and Thompson says rules written to protect the environment in the 1970s now block the clean energy and housing needed today.

quotes.text: needs thoroughgoing reform so that we can build things cheaper and faster
quotes.where: Saldin and Teles, climate paragraph, line 69 of the saved text

quotes.text: the same rules that were designed to help the environment in the 1960s and 1970s are sometimes ironically used in a way that hurt the environment in the 2020s. And that’s one reason why, we, as liberals need a paradigm shift.
quotes.where: Lex Fridman interview, Thompson, 01:49:54, line 531 of the saved text

notes: The record is narrow: Klein and Thompson's Abundance book text could not be opened (no open-access copy), so the audit rests on their long interview, a political-science essay, a defence of the view by a journalist. Themes searched in those sources and in the Niskanen playbook and cost-disease pages: housing and zoning, energy, climate, nuclear, science funding, state capacity and procedure, redistribution and tax credits, health-care supply, regulation, unions, immigration, trade, courts and elections, culture and religion, foreign policy and defence. Immigration, trade and health-care supply appear only in passing or in sources about a wider movement (Niskanen), so they stay null. Klein's and Thompson's views on Trump, DOGE and the Democratic Party are outside the scope. Whaples's Independent Review book review was read but is not cited, since it does not name the ideology.
